Neutron-star cooling: how much do pairing gaps, envelope and mass move the curves?

Working report, 19–20 November 2026. 164 runs of the neutron-star-cooling solver: a 67-run sweep over gaps, envelope and mass (sections 1–5), a 50-run mass sweep with the default microphysics (section 6), and 47 follow-up runs that fill the remaining gaps (section 7). Compared with the ns-thermal-catalogue review values of 19 November 2026.

The five reference cooling curves used in the catalogue differed from each other by up to a factor of ten at 1–30 kyr. This sweep shows that the difference comes mainly from the pairing gaps and the envelope, not from the equation of state. It also gives a minimal-cooling band against which the observed sources can be tested.

Main results

Without direct Urca, the core neutron-triplet gap is the dominant choice, followed by the core proton gap and the envelope composition. For a given gap setting with no triplet gap, EOS and mass shift the curves by at most about 0.5 dex. When a triplet gap is present, mass also moves the time of the pair-breaking drop, and that can change L at a given age by about 1 dex (section 6).

The lower edge of the minimal-cooling band is robust. It is the same within 0.06 dex across 11 published triplet gap models.

With the default gaps, mass changes the curves mainly by shifting when the triplet pair-breaking drop happens. That is why the original five reference curves at 1.4 M☉ looked so different from each other.

Against that band, PSR J0007+7303 is the only source that is clearly too cold: at least 1.1 dex below. Vela Jr and J0205+6449 are marginally below (about 0.2 dex). B1727−47 is below only if its envelope is iron.

Direct Urca reaches J0007 only where the region in which it operates is not covered by pairing. A heavy mass alone is not enough: with the cold-reference gaps, BSk24 stays above the J0007 limit at every mass up to 1.95 M☉.

The follow-up runs confirm both band edges to within about 0.1 dex. The references are numerically converged. Passive cooling can reach every independent-age source older than 105 yr, including B0950+08.

1. What was run

All runs use the solver as published: mesh C, initial redshifted temperature 1010 K, B = 0, the Yakovlev et al. (2001) modified Urca rates and BCF2024 bremsstrahlung. Each run stops when Lγ∞ falls below 1030 erg/s. The crust neutron gap is fixed to the default (model 7), because the solver’s own earlier scan showed it changes L by at most 6%.

Direct Urca opens at 1.15 M☉ for BSk22, 1.60 for BSk24, 1.63 for BSk25 and 1.98 for APR, and never for BSk26, whose maximum mass is 2.17 M☉. Throughout, “minimal cooling” means every run below its EOS threshold.

Each run took 19–51 s on one core, about 35 minutes in total. Every run closed its energy balance; the largest error was 1.5% against a 2% tolerance, and the median was 0.02%. Per-run details are in tables/run_qc.csv.

2. Pairing gaps and envelope in a single star

The proton gap sets the overall level. A strong proton gap suppresses modified Urca throughout the core and raises L by about a factor of 4 at 104 yr (log L 33.93 compared with 33.33 with no proton gap). The weak AO proton gap is close to having no gap at all.

The triplet gap sets the drops. Each sharp fall in panel (a) is the onset of pair-breaking emission, when the core temperature falls below the critical temperature of the triplet gap. With the high-Tc AO gap this happens before 300 yr. With the low BEEHS gap it happens near 103 yr without proton pairing, but only at 1–3 × 104 yr with a strong proton gap. That interaction is why gap channels cannot be scanned one at a time. Once their drop has happened, all combinations with a triplet gap lie within about 0.3 dex of each other (log L 32.4–32.7 at 3 × 104 yr).

This also explains the original five reference curves. With the default deep triplet gap, the critical temperature reached inside the star depends on the central density. It is 0.41 × 109 K in BSk24 but 0.92 × 109 K in APR, so the drop happens at about 3 × 104 yr in one and about 300 yr in the other. The apparent EOS dependence was really a gap-placement effect.

The envelope effect reverses with age (panel b). An accreted (light-element) envelope has a higher surface temperature for the same base temperature. It is therefore 0.5–0.8 dex brighter while the star is cooled mainly by neutrinos, but it then cools faster once photons dominate. The crossover is near 105 yr for weakly paired stars and near 2 × 104 yr for strongly paired ones, whose heat capacity is small. The extreme case, strong proton plus high triplet gap with an accreted envelope, falls below 1030 erg/s by 80 kyr. The run with the original default gaps reproduces the existing BSk24 reference curve within 0.07 dex.

3. Mass and equation of state

Without direct Urca, EOS and mass matter little (solid lines). In the cold setting, every star without direct Urca lies within about 0.1 dex up to 104 yr. In the hot setting the two heaviest stars without direct Urca, BSk26 at 2.1 M☉ and APR at 1.7 M☉, form a second family about 0.4 dex lower. The strong proton gap only extends to kF ≈ 1.3 fm−1, so their dense centres keep unsuppressed modified Urca.

With direct Urca, “hot” and “cold” swap. The proton gap does not reach the dense centre where direct Urca operates, but the high triplet gap does, and suppresses it there. So in heavy stars the nominally hot setting (dashed lines in a) is the colder of the two. For example, BSk24 at 1.7 M☉ has log L 30.99 at 104 yr in the hot setting and 31.90 in the cold one. With no gaps at all, BSk22 at 1.4 M☉ falls below 1030 erg/s by 22 kyr.

The transition is sharp. BSk24 gives log L 32.70 at 1.55 M☉ and 31.5–32.0 at 1.65 M☉, a change of about 1 dex for 0.1 M☉. In practice there is no lower floor once direct Urca is allowed: some heavy, weakly paired star can always explain a cold source. The physically informative comparison is therefore with the minimal-cooling band.

4. How robust is the cold edge?

The cold edge comes from one gap model, so it was tested against ten alternatives. AO stays the coldest from 3 × 103 yr onwards. Before that, HGA12-deep is lower by only 0.06 dex. So the cold edge is essentially independent of which published triplet gap is assumed.

A larger gap does not give a colder star. The Baldo model (peak Tc 5.4 × 109 K) pairs the whole core so early that the pair-breaking emission is over before the ages that matter, and then suppressed. The coldest models are those whose pair-breaking emission is strongest at the relevant ages, here AO and TToa.

At the other extreme, EEHOr (peak Tc 0.17 × 109 K) is barely active and stays near the hot reference until about 105 yr. Most of the width of the minimal-cooling band therefore comes from a single microphysical uncertainty: the strength and density profile of the core neutron-triplet gap.

5. The bands compared with the sources

A source counts as below the band only if its whole error box lies below the band at every age in its range. Upper limits are treated as boxes extending to zero luminosity.

J0007+7303 is the robust case. Even if its luminosity ceiling were 2–3 times higher, which is plausible given the spectral model, it would still lie at least about 0.6 dex below the band. That requires enhanced cooling, for example direct Urca in a heavier star.

Vela Jr and J0205+6449 are marginal. They are about 0.17–0.18 dex below, which is within their distance and emitting-component systematics. For J0205 the lower part of the box comes from a small-area hot-spot fit, which is not a measurement of cooling luminosity.

B1727−47 depends on the envelope. With an accreted envelope, the strongly paired cold edge drops fast enough after 3 × 104 yr to reach its upper limit.

B2334+61 depends on the distance branch. It is inside the band with the current hybrid box, which pairs the near-distance age with the far-distance luminosity. On the self-consistent near-distance branch (about 7.7 kyr) it would be 0.8–1.3 dex below: 0.8 dex with the whole-surface atmosphere fit that is valid near 1 kpc, more with the hot-spot interpretation. On the far branch its age is unknown but probably older, and it would be inside. This is the first source to discuss next.

No source is above the band. Cas A is inside it, but at ages where several triplet gap models produce their pair-breaking drop (Figure 3), so it is the source most sensitive to that choice. S147, the most luminous source near 30 kyr, sits well inside the band, about 0.8 dex below the Fe hot edge.

6. Mass sweep with the default microphysics

This second sweep isolates the effect of mass. All microphysics stays at the solver defaults used for the original five reference curves: crust neutron gap 7, core triplet gap 12 (HGA12 deep), core proton gap 8 (HGA12 ≈ CCDK), the Gudmundsson envelope, and mesh C. Each EOS was run at ten masses evenly spaced from 1.2 to 2.0 M☉, 50 runs in total. All runs completed; the largest energy-closure error was 0.48% and the median 0.07%. The whole sweep took about 27 minutes of solver time on one core.

APR32.9032.9132.9332.9432.9632.9732.9933.0033.0132.26

BSk26 and APR: mass only moves the pair-breaking drop. The default triplet gap grows with density, so heavier stars reach a larger critical temperature in their centre and enter pair-breaking cooling earlier. The drop moves from about 1.5 kyr at 1.2 M☉ to before 100 yr at 2.0 M☉. After about 5 kyr all masses converge, within 0.05 dex at 104 yr. In the photon era the heavier stars cool slightly faster. The single APR run above its threshold (2.0 M☉, threshold 1.98 M☉) has direct Urca and drops to 1.8 × 1032 erg/s at 104 yr.

BSk24 and BSk25: two effects stacked. These EOS reach lower central densities at a given mass. Up to about 1.4 M☉ the critical temperature of the default triplet gap inside the star stays low, the drop comes late, and the star stays on a hot plateau of about 1034 erg/s at 104 yr. Between about 1.3 and 1.6 M☉ the drop moves steadily earlier, which produces the staircase of curves in panels 2 and 3. Above the direct Urca thresholds (1.60 and 1.63 M☉), L at 104 yr falls to about 9 × 1031 erg/s and then hardly changes with mass. The proton and triplet gaps keep suppressing direct Urca in part of the region where it operates.

BSk22: direct Urca everywhere in the grid. All ten masses are above its 1.15 M☉ threshold. Near the threshold, the region where direct Urca operates is small and largely covered by the gaps, so its suppression fades gradually with mass. L at 104 yr falls from 9 × 1032 erg/s at 1.2 M☉ to a floor of about 2.5 × 1031 erg/s from about 1.5 M☉ upwards.

What this means for the original reference curves. At 1.4 M☉, BSk24 and BSk25 happen to sit on their hot plateau, while BSk26 and APR have already had their early drop. A star only 0.2 M☉ heavier would reverse the order. The factor-of-ten difference between the original curves is therefore not a property of the equations of state as such. It reflects where 1.4 M☉ falls relative to the density profile of the triplet gap, and for BSk24 and BSk25 how close it is to the direct Urca threshold. Comparing a source against one curve per EOS at a single mass can therefore suggest an EOS preference that the physics does not support.

Implications for the cold sources, with the default microphysics only.

  • J0007+7303 (below 3 × 1031 erg/s at about 104 yr) is reached only by BSk22 at about 1.5 M☉ or more. With these gaps, direct Urca in BSk24 and BSk25 levels off at about 9 × 1031 erg/s, still too warm. In the gap sweep of sections 2–3, direct Urca without gaps went much lower, so this conclusion depends on the default gap choice.
  • The B2334+61 near-distance branch ((1.2–8.2) × 1031 erg/s at about 8 kyr) can be matched by direct Urca in BSk22, BSk24 or BSk25.

7. Follow-up runs: filling the remaining gaps

After sections 1–6, five things were still open: the cold edge had been tested at only two central densities; the hot edge rested on a single proton gap; the direct Urca regime was coarsely sampled; no curve went below 1030 erg/s; and the references had not been checked numerically. These 47 runs address each of those. All completed. The largest energy-closure error was 0.62% (median 0.02%), and the total solver time was 33 minutes.

G12Which proton gap gives the hottest star?Proton gaps CCDK, BCLL, CCYms, EEHO, EEHOr and T, with no triplet gap and an Fe envelope, in BSk24 at 1.2 M☉ and BSk26 at 2.1 M☉
H11What does direct Urca need to reach the cold sources?BSk24 at 1.62, 1.66, 1.75 and 1.95 M☉, without gaps and with the cold-reference gaps; BSk22 without gaps at 1.2, 1.3 and 1.5 M☉
I4Do the results survive a light-element envelope?Accreted versions of the cold reference, the hot setting in a light star, and the two BSk24 1.75 M☉ runs from block H

7.1 The cold edge holds at other central densities

From 3 to 30 kyr, no run in panel (a) falls more than 0.02 dex below the cold reference. The largest deviations are about 0.1 dex. Below 1 kyr, the AO gap in the light BSk24 star is lower (log L 33.08 against 33.17 at 103 yr). At 105 yr, TToa in BSk26 at 1.6 M☉ is 0.07 dex lower. These shifts are too small to change any verdict.

The HGA12-deep gap (purple) shows the central-density effect of section 6 clearly. In the light BSk24 star its gap is never reached and the star stays near the hot edge. At 1.5 M☉ the drop comes at about 104 yr, and in BSk26 at 1.6 M☉ it comes before 300 yr.

7.2 The hot edge holds across proton gaps

CCDK reproduces the reference gap (model 8) to plotting precision, as expected from their near-identical parameters. All five other proton gaps are colder. In the light star the difference at 104 yr is 0.08 dex (EEHO) to 0.37 dex (BCLL), because they cover less of the core. In the heavy star the difference is at most 0.03 dex: its dense centre lies beyond the reach of every proton gap, so modified Urca there is unsuppressed whatever the choice. The hot edge is therefore set by the broadest strong proton gap, which is the one already used.

7.3 What direct Urca needs to explain the cold sources

Without gaps, direct Urca overshoots. BSk24 just above its threshold (1.62 M☉) gives log L 30.95 at 104 yr, about 0.5 dex below the J0007 limit (31.48). Heavier stars go lower still. BSk22 without gaps gives 30.55 already at 1.2 M☉.

With the cold-reference gaps, direct Urca falls short. The AO triplet gap covers the whole region where direct Urca operates. BSk24 then only falls from 31.94 at 1.62 M☉ to 31.65 at 1.95 M☉, never reaching the J0007 limit.

The default gaps reach J0007 only in BSk22. BSk22 at 1.5 M☉ or more levels off at log L ≈ 31.40, just below the limit. Its direct Urca region begins at low density (0.33 fm−3), where the deep default triplet gap is absent. In BSk24 and BSk25 the default gaps level off at about 31.95, above the limit.

So J0007 needs direct Urca in a region that pairing leaves largely uncovered. That can mean weak gaps, or an EOS whose direct Urca region lies outside the triplet gap. A heavy mass alone is not enough.

This conclusion depends on the catalogue’s luminosity ceiling. If the blackbody-based ceiling of about 1032 erg/s were adopted instead (see the J0007 entry in the catalogue review), the cold-reference gaps in BSk24 above about 1.6 M☉ would also be compatible. The spectral question for J0007 therefore decides how strong a constraint it places on pairing.

The B2334+61 near branch ((1.2–8.2) × 1031 erg/s) is much easier to reach. BSk24 with the cold-reference gaps does so from about 1.66 M☉, and BSk22 with the default gaps from about 1.45 M☉.

Accreted envelope: it raises the direct Urca stars by 0.5–0.6 dex at 104 yr. BSk24 at 1.75 M☉ without gaps still lies below the J0007 limit (31.04). With the cold-reference gaps it rises to 32.25, well above the limit.

7.4 Late times

The four references reach 1029 erg/s at very different ages:

  • hot reference, Fe: 3.7 Myr (1028 erg/s at 4.3 Myr);
  • hot reference, accreted: 0.97 Myr;
  • cold reference, Fe: 0.42 Myr;
  • cold reference, accreted: 0.12 Myr.

Every independent-age source older than 105 yr lies between the references. That includes B0950+08 (8 × 1028 erg/s, 0.6–7.6 Myr), which passive cooling can therefore accommodate. This comparison alone does not require internal heating.

Two XINS with only characteristic ages lie above every passive curve: RX J2143.0+0654 (9 × 1031 erg/s at τc = 3.7 Myr) and RX J0806.4−4123 (2 × 1031 erg/s at 17 Myr). For the three XINS with independent ages, τc exceeds the true age by 2–9 times. At a fifth of their characteristic ages, both would lie inside the band, so their position here says more about τc than about cooling.

The small-hot-spot pulsars older than about 4 Myr also lie above the hot reference. That is expected, since their emission is polar-cap heating rather than surface cooling.

Below 1030 erg/s only the four references were followed, so the lower edge of the band is not defined there.

7.5 Numerical checks

  • Mesh: on mesh D, both references change by at most 0.005 dex anywhere between 300 yr and 0.3 Myr.
  • Initial temperature: starting at 109 K instead of 1010 K changes the curves by 0.02–0.03 dex at 30 yr and by less than 0.002 dex from 100 yr onwards.

The results are converged and independent of the initial condition at every age where sources exist.

7.6 Updated bands and verdicts

The bands in Figure 4 are rebuilt from all 164 runs, except the numerical checks. The mass-sweep runs, with the Gudmundsson envelope, count as iron-like.

  • The Fe lower edge moves by at most 0.07 dex up to 105 yr: 0.02 dex lower at 103 yr and 0.07 dex lower at 105 yr.
  • The Fe upper edge rises by at most 0.04 dex, from BSk25 at 1.38 M☉ with the default gaps.
  • The source verdicts are unchanged, except that Vela Jr moves from 0.19 to 0.17 dex below the band. The updated comparison is in tables/source_verdicts_v2.txt.

8. Reference models

ReferenceDefinitionHow closely it follows the band edge
Cold (minimal cooling)Strong proton gap (HGA12≈CCDK) + AO triplet gap; BSk26, 2.1 M☉; Fe envelope. For the light-element case, the accreted version is colder after about 2 × 104 yr.Within 0.18 dex of the Fe lower edge at all ages (rms 0.06 dex); stable across 11 triplet models
Hot (minimal cooling)Strong proton gap, no triplet gap; BSk26, 1.7 M☉. Accreted envelope up to about 1.5 × 105 yr, Fe afterwards.Within 0.49 dex as a single Fe run (rms 0.38). Only the composite follows the hot edge at all ages.

The follow-up runs (section 7) confirm both references: the cold edge holds across four more triplet gaps at three more central densities, and the hot edge across six proton gaps. Both are numerically converged.

The two references differ essentially in one choice: whether the core neutrons pair into a triplet state with a gap large enough to trigger pair-breaking emission at the relevant ages. Neither was tuned to the observed sources.

9. Limitations

  • In total, 7 of the solver’s 12 proton gaps and 11 of its triplet gaps were sampled. Not every combination of gap, mass and EOS was run.
  • The magnetic field is zero. Only fully iron and fully accreted envelopes were run, with no partially accreted cases.
  • The solver’s documented approximations remain: the pair-breaking response, the APR crust composition, and the BSk25 and BSk26 table rows omitted by the reader. Mesh convergence was checked only for the two references (section 7.5).
  • The mass sweep uses one set of gaps and one envelope. Its quantitative statements, such as the levels after direct Urca switches on, hold for the default microphysics only.
  • Below 1030 erg/s, only the four reference runs of block J extend; the band itself is not defined there.
  • The source boxes are the catalogue’s current working values. Their own open issues (hot-spot versus whole-surface components, distance branches) are discussed in the catalogue audit and affect the verdicts above.

Contents of this folder

  • report.html: this report, with the figures embedded.
  • figures/: the eight figures as separate PNG files.
  • tables/run_table.csv: one row per run, giving its settings, direct-Urca flag, log L at eight ages and final age.
  • tables/cooling_sweep_curves.csv: all 67 cooling curves, in the same format as cooling_five_eos.csv in the catalogue.
  • tables/bands.csv: the upper and lower edges of the three bands on a common age grid.
  • tables/run_qc.csv: runtime and energy-closure error per run.
  • tables/source_verdicts.txt: the source comparison.
  • tables/plan.csv: the run plan.
  • tables/mass_sweep_table.csv, tables/mass_sweep_curves.csv, tables/mass_sweep_qc.csv: the 50-run mass sweep, giving log L at eight ages per run, the full curves, and runtime and energy closure.
  • tables/followup_run_table.csv, tables/followup_curves.csv, tables/followup_qc.csv: the 47 follow-up runs of blocks F–K.
  • tables/bands_v2.csv: the bands rebuilt from all runs, with the run that defines each edge at each age. tables/bands.csv is the earlier version from the first sweep. tables/source_verdicts_v2.txt is the updated source comparison.
  • runs_inputs/gap_sweep/ (67 files), runs_inputs/mass_sweep/ (50 files) and runs_inputs/followup_sweep/ (47 files): the solver input files.
  • scripts/: plan, runner, analysis and plotting scripts for both sweeps (the mass sweep uses run_mass.py and plot_mass.py). These expect the solver repository next to the sweep folder.
